title: Philo, Aristobulus and Numenius
source_text: Δοκεῖ δέ μοι καὶ ἀκηκοέναι ὅτι ἐστὶ συγγράμματα περιέχοντα τὰς τοῦ νόμου ἀλληγορίας, ἅπερ εἰ ἀνεγνώκει, οὐκ ἂν ἔλεγεν· αἱ γοῦν δοκοῦσαι περὶ αὐτῶν ἀλληγορίαι γεγράφθαι πολὺ τῶν μύθων αἰσχίους εἰσὶ καὶ ἀτοπώτεραι, τὰ μηδαμῆ μηδαμῶς ἁρμοσθῆναι δυνάμενα θαυμαστῇ τινι καὶ παντάπασιν ἀναισθήτῳ μωρίᾳ συνάπτουσαι. ἔοικε δὲ περὶ τῶν Φίλωνος συγγραμμάτων ταῦτα λέγειν ἢ καὶ τῶν ἔτι ἀρχαιοτέρων, ὁποῖά ἐστι τὰ Ἀριστοβούλου. στοχάζομαι δὲ τὸν Κέλσον μὴ ἀνεγνωκέναι τὰ βιβλία, ἐπεὶ πολλαχοῦ οὕτως ἐπιτετεῦχθαί μοι φαίνεται, ὥστε αἱρεθῆναι ἂν καὶ τοὺς ἐν Ἕλλησι φιλοσοφοῦντας ἀπὸ τῶν λεγομένων· ἐν οἷς οὐ μόνον φράσις ἐξήσκηται ἀλλὰ καὶ νοήματα καὶ δόγματα καὶ ἡ χρῆσις τῶν, ὡς οἴεται, ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν μύθων ὁ Κέλσος. ἐγὼ δ᾿ οἶδα καὶ Νουμήνιον τὸν Πυθαγόρειον. ἄνδρα πολλῷ κρεῖττον διηγησάμενον Πλάτωνα καὶ (περὶ) τῶν Πυθαγορείων δογμάτων πρεσβεύσαντα, πολλαχοῦ τῶν συγγραμμάτων αὐτοῦ ἐκτιθέμενον τὰ Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν προφητῶν καὶ οὐκ ἀπιθάνως αὐτὰ τροπολογοῦντα, ὥσπερ ἐν τῷ καλουμένῳ Ἔποπι καὶ ἐν τοῖς περὶ ἀριθμῶν καὶ ἐν τοῖς περὶ τόπου. ἐν δὲ τῷ τρίτῳ περὶ τἀγαθοῦ ἐκτίθεται καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἱστορίαν τινὰ, τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ οὐ λέγων, καὶ τροπολογεῖ αὐτήν· πότερον δ᾿ ἐπιτετευγμένως ἢ ἀποτετευγμένως, ἄλλου καιροῦ ἐστιν εἰπεῖν. ἐκτίθεται καὶ τὴν περὶ Μωϋσέως καὶ Ἰαννοῦ καὶ Ἰαμβροῦ ἱστορίαν. ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἐν ἐκείνῃ σεμνυνόμεθα, ἀποδεχόμεθα δ᾿ αὐτὸν μᾶλλον Κέλσου καὶ ἄλλων Ἑλλήνων βουληθέντα φιλομαθῶς καὶ τὰ ἡμέτερα ἐξετάσαι καὶ κινηθέντα ὡς περὶ τροπολογουμένων καὶ οὐ μωρῶν συγγραμμάτων.
pass_a_gloss: He seems to me also to have heard that there are writings (σύγγραμμα) containing the allegories of the law; which if he had read, he would not have said: 'at any rate the allegories seeming to have been written about them are much more shameful (αἰσχίων) than the myths and more absurd (ἀτοπώτερος), joining (συνάπτω) things in no way at all able to be fitted together (ἁρμόζω) with a marvellous and altogether senseless (ἀναίσθητος) folly (μωρία).' He seems to say these things about the writings of Philo or of still more ancient men, such as those of Aristobulus. I conjecture (στοχάζομαι) that Celsus has not read the books, since in many places they seem to me so successful (ἐπιτυγχάνω) that even those philosophizing among the Greeks would be captured (αἱρέω, passive) by what is said; in which not only phrasing (φράσις) has been worked out (ἐξασκέω) but also thoughts (νόημα) and doctrines (δόγμα) and the use (χρῆσις) of the myths, as Celsus thinks, from the Scriptures. I know also Numenius the Pythagorean, a man who expounded (διηγέομαι) Plato much better and championed (πρεσβεύω) [the] Pythagorean doctrines, in many places of his writings setting out (ἐκτίθημι) the things of Moses and the prophets and not unpersuasively (οὐκ ἀπιθάνως) interpreting them figuratively (τροπολογέω), as in the so-called Epops (Hoopoe) and in those On Numbers and On Place. In the third On the Good he sets out also a certain story about Jesus, not saying his name, and interprets it figuratively; whether successfully or unsuccessfully (ἐπιτετευγμένως / ἀποτετευγμένως), it is for another occasion (καιρός) to say. He sets out also the story about Moses and Jannes and Jambres. But we do not pride ourselves (σεμνύνομαι) on that; but we approve (ἀποδέχομαι) him more than Celsus and other Greeks, as having wished with love of learning (φιλομαθῶς) to examine also our things and been moved (κινέω) as about figuratively interpreted and not foolish (μωρός) writings.
pass_b_english: He also seems to me to have heard that there are writings containing allegories of the law. If he had read them, he would not have said: “At any rate, the allegories that are thought to have been written about them are far more shameful and absurd than the myths, for they join together, with an astonishing and utterly senseless folly, things that can in no way whatever be fitted together.” He seems to say this about the writings of Philo, or even of men still more ancient, such as the writings of Aristobulus. But I conjecture that Celsus has not read these books, since in many places they seem to me so successful that even the philosophers among the Greeks would be won over by what they say. In them not only is the style carefully worked, but so also are the thoughts, the doctrines, and the use made of what Celsus takes to be myths from the Scriptures.

I know also of Numenius the Pythagorean, a man who expounded Plato far better and who championed the doctrines of the Pythagoreans. In many places in his writings he sets out passages of Moses and the prophets and gives them a figurative interpretation that is not unpersuasive, as in the work called The Hoopoe, and in the books On Numbers and On Place. In the third book On the Good he even sets out a story about Jesus, without saying his name, and interprets it figuratively; whether successfully or not is a question for another time. He also sets out the story about Moses and Jannes and Jambres (Exodus 7:11; 2 Timothy 3:8). We do not take pride in that; but we do welcome him more than Celsus and other Greeks, because out of love of learning he was willing to examine our writings as well, and was moved by them as writings to be read figuratively and not as foolish ones.

choices.choice: ἢ καί: 'or even of men still more ancient'
ἐπιτετευγμένως ἢ ἀποτετευγμένως: 'whether successfully or not' (was ambiguous 'with success or without it is')
word order: 'He also sets out the story'
Exodus 7:11 and 2 Timothy 3:8 checked (Jannes and Jambres named only in 2 Timothy)

Celsus's περὶ αὐτῶν ('about them') refers to the biblical stories under discussion. 'Far better' (πολλῷ κρεῖττον) has no stated comparison; probably 'far better than Celsus'; the comparative is kept bare as in the Greek. (περὶ) before τῶν Πυθαγορείων δογμάτων is an editorial supplement in the copy-text; the sense 'championed the Pythagorean doctrines' stands either way. Titles of Numenius's works (Epops, Peri arithmōn, Peri topou, Peri tagathou book 3) are given in English. The Jannes and Jambres story is not named in Exodus; they are the Egyptian magicians of Exodus 7:11, named in 2 Timothy 3:8; cited as an allusion. ἐν ἐκείνῃ (feminine) most likely refers to that story (ἱστορία), i.e. we do not pride ourselves on Numenius's telling of it; rendered neutrally as 'in that'.
